summary: Nevada is permissive and the roof rat is almost certainly fine — but there's a wording gap. NRS 501.097 defines 'wildlife' to include wild mammals 'whether raised in captivity or not,' and the key exemption (NAC 503.140) frees 'domesticated races of rats and mice' from any NDOW permit. R. rattus is NOT on Nevada's prohibited-species list (only the African multimammate rat is). The open question is whether NDOW reads 'domesticated races of rats' to include captive-bred R. rattus (it clearly covers the fancy rat). If yes — as is likely — keeping, breeding, selling, and transporting are fully legal with no permit. We've asked NDOW to confirm.

kit.problem: In Nevada, keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is almost certainly already legal. The roof rat is not on Nevada's prohibited-species list (NAC 503.110 lists only the African multimammate rat, Mastomys), and NAC 503.140 exempts "domesticated races of rats and mice" from any Nevada Department of Wildlife (NDOW) permit or license. That is the same rule that covers the ordinary pet "fancy rat." No law bans the animal. The single gap is a wording question. Nevada's wildlife definition (NRS 501.097) includes wild mammals "whether raised in captivity or not." NDOW has not published anything confirming that its "domesticated races of rats and mice" exemption reaches captive-bred R. rattus specifically; the exemption clearly covers R. norvegicus, the fancy rat. Until NDOW confirms this in writing, an owner, breeder, or seller of pet roof rats cannot be certain whether a possession license or importation permit is required, even though the natural reading is that multi-generational, captive-bred, tame roof rats are the "domesticated races of rats" the regulation already exempts.
kit.ask: Ask NDOW to confirm in writing that the NAC 503.140 exemption for "domesticated races of rats and mice" includes captive-bred Rattus rattus kept as companion animals, so that possessing, breeding, gifting or selling, and importing pet roof rats requires no NDOW permit or license, the same as for the fancy rat. The phrase turns on domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness. The already-exempt pet "fancy rat" is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over: a "domesticated race of rats" in the same sense. That is the reading NDOW is asked to confirm, not a conclusion it is asked to reach. A written confirmation or declaratory ruling closes the gap. If NDOW will not read the existing exemption that way, ask it to bring a rule petition to the Board of Wildlife Commissioners to add R. rattus by name to the NAC 503.140 exemption list. Separately, ask the Nevada Department of Agriculture whether any certificate of veterinary inspection or entry permit applies to a small pet rodent brought into Nevada. On domestication background, see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.
kit.branch_note: This is an agency-clarification lever, not a legislative one. The roof rat is not on any statutory or regulatory prohibited list, so there is no bad law to repeal, and appealing to the Legislature would target a ban that does not exist. The obstacle is interpretive: whether NDOW reads its own existing exemption (NAC 503.140, "domesticated races of rats and mice") to reach captive-bred R. rattus. The exemption text and the absence of R. rattus from the NAC 503.110 prohibited list both point toward legal, so the correct first move is to ask NDOW for a written confirmation or declaratory ruling that the exemption covers the captive-bred roof rat. The agency can do this without any new rule. The optional second-line lever is quasi-legislative within the agency. If NDOW declines to confirm by interpretation, a member of the public can petition the Board of Wildlife Commissioners (the body that adopts and amends NAC wildlife regulations) to add R. rattus by name to the NAC 503.140 exemption, a rulemaking route rather than an ordinary statute. The request is not to override a law NDOW is correctly applying, but to map an exemption it already administers onto a species the law does not prohibit. Kept that modest, it is well within NDOW's authority.

The form is preferable; ndowinfo@ndow.org is the verified general inbox if you'd rather email.

template.en:
To the Nevada Department of Wildlife, Wildlife Diversity Division:

I am writing to ask for a written clarification about pet roof rats (Rattus rattus). I keep these animals as companion pets and want to be sure I am following Nevada law.

Roof rats kept as pets are captive-bred over many generations, hand-tame, housed indoors in cages, and never released into the wild. They are kept the same way as the ordinary pet "fancy rat" (Rattus norvegicus).

My question is one of wording, not of any ban. R. rattus is not on the NAC 503.110 prohibited-species list, and NAC 503.140 already exempts "domesticated races of rats and mice" from any NDOW permit or license. Captive-bred pet roof rats appear to be such a "domesticated race of rats." What makes an animal a domesticated race is its breeding history, not its wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over.

Please confirm in writing that the NAC 503.140 exemption includes captive-bred Rattus rattus kept as companion animals, so that possessing, breeding, gifting, and importing them requires no NDOW permit or license. If NDOW reads the exemption otherwise, would it consider a rule petition to add R. rattus by name to that list?

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, Nevada]
[Your email / phone]

kit.confidence_notes: Verified on official NDOW pages (June 2026): the general agency inbox ndowinfo@ndow.org and the live contact form at https://www.ndow.org/contact-us/, which lets you route an inquiry to the Wildlife Diversity division. Verified across multiple official Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners meeting agendas that wildlifecommission@ndow.org is the correct address for written public comment and for support material/petition correspondence to the Commission (the body that adopts/amends NAC wildlife regulations). The legal substance is from prior research grounded in NRS 501.097, NAC 503.140, and NAC 503.110 via leg.state.nv.us and Cornell LII. NOT independently re-verified in this pass and flagged uncertain: (1) the exact current text of NAC 503.140 and whether NDOW has any newer published guidance; (2) whether an NDOW importation permit/CVI applies to pet rodents; (3) the Nevada Department of Agriculture entry-permit email (entrypermits@agri.nv.gov) and phone are carried from the jurisdiction file and were not re-checked here. Local Clark County/Las Vegas/Henderson business or breeder permits may apply to commercial activity regardless of species. This is a research aid, not legal advice; confirm current rules with the agencies before relying on them.

keep.why: NAC 503.140 exempts 'domesticated races of rats and mice' from NDOW possession licensing; if captive-bred R. rattus is a 'domesticated race,' no license is needed. R. rattus is not on the NAC 503.110 prohibited list (only Mastomys is), so prohibition is unlikely — but NDOW hasn't published a ruling confirming the exemption reaches R. rattus specifically (vs. just R. norvegicus). Likely legal; confirm with NDOW.
keep.governing_law: NRS 501.097 (wildlife defn incl. captive-bred); NAC 503.140 (exempt 'domesticated races of rats and mice'); NAC 503.110 (prohibited list).

breed.why: If R. rattus qualifies under the NAC 503.140 exemption, breeding needs no NDOW permit; if not, a NAC 504 possession license would apply. No species-specific breeding prohibition exists. Commercial-scale operations may need a local business/breeder permit regardless of species.
breed.governing_law: NAC 503.140; NAC 504 (possession license framework); local breeder ordinances.

sell_give.why: NAC 503.140 expressly allows lawfully-acquired exempt species to be sold in Nevada without an NDOW dealer permit; if R. rattus is within 'domesticated races,' private sale/free adoption is fine. Local business licenses apply to commercial activity.
sell_give.governing_law: NAC 503.140 (sale of exempt species); NAC 504; local ordinances.

transport.why: NAC 503.140 species may be transported and imported without an NDOW permit/CVI; if R. rattus is exempt, no importation permit is needed. If treated as non-exempt wildlife, an NDOW importation permit + CVI would apply. The NDA's separate import rules don't appear to require a CVI for small pet rodents — confirm. Never release (R. rattus is a pest under NRS 567).
transport.governing_law: NRS 503.597 / NAC 503 (importation permit); NAC 503.140 (import exemption for listed species); NDA import rules.

restrictions.summary: Never release a roof rat — it's treated as a pest in the wild (NRS 567). Local (Clark County / Las Vegas / Henderson) business or breeder permits apply to commercial activity regardless of species.

inquiry_focus: Does NDOW interpret the phrase 'domesticated races of rats and mice' in NAC 503.140 to include multi-generational captive-bred Rattus rattus (roof rat) kept as companion animals — so that possession, breeding, sale/gift, and interstate import require no NDOW permit or license (the same practical status as Rattus norvegicus)? If NDOW instead treats R. rattus as regulated wildlife under the NRS 501.097 definition, what permit (NAC 504) applies, and would NDOW consider a rule petition to name R. rattus within the NAC 503.140 exemption? Separately, does the Dept of Agriculture require a CVI/import permit for a pet rodent entering Nevada?
